Reference: Harstad (2024)

Model Setting

The paper builds a deliberately simple dynamic game to show how international trade and the exploitation of a depletable natural resource interact, and how trade policy can be redesigned to reverse the negative interactions. The South (SSS) owns a resource stock (the leading example is a tropical rainforest), and the North (NNN) suffers a damage whenever the resource is exploited. Logging produces timber and converts forest into agricultural land (beef), and both products can be exported to NNN. The motivating episode is the 2019 EU–Mercosur agreement, concluded while deforestation in the Amazon was rising, and the 2020 proposal by France and the Netherlands to link tariff reductions to the implementation of sustainability provisions.

The paper delivers two sets of results. Under a standard free trade agreement (FTA), (1) trade causes exploitation, because export prices exceed domestic valuations; (2) exploitation causes trade, because an FTA is only socially valuable once little resource is left to lose; and (3) SSS exploits in order to obtain trade, so the parties end up trading and depleting even when the damage exceeds the gains from trade. Under a contingent trade agreement (CTA), in which tariffs are functions of the remaining stock and are renegotiation proof, all these results are reversed: SSS faces low tariffs while the stock is large and high tariffs if it shrinks, so conservation is rewarded with a larger share of the gains from trade. Combined with export subsidies by NNN, the CTA implements the first best; without subsidies, conservation is limited by the size of the gains from trade.

The key idea, borrowed from dynamic games with renegotiation, is that punishments must stay on the Pareto frontier: after exploitation the parties still trade, but the gains are reallocated toward the harmed party. This is nontrivial because the ex post frontier expands as the resource is depleted.

Rt+1=Rt−xt,Xt+1=Xt+xt,Xt+Rt=R0(9.5.2.1)R_{t+1}=R_t-x_t,\qquad X_{t+1}=X_t+x_t,\qquad X_t+R_t=R_0 \tag{9.5.2.1}Rt+1​=Rt​−xt​,Xt+1​=Xt​+xt​,Xt​+Rt​=R0​(9.5.2.1)

First Best and Bargaining

Utilities are transferable, so the per-period gains from trade are the first expression below. To have an environmental problem, the paper assumes (second expression) that the total value of exploitation, even when the products are traded, is below its social cost:

(1−δ)e+(1−δ)(aˉ−a‾)(Xt+xt)+(bˉ−b‾)xt>0,aˉ+bˉ<c+d(9.5.2.5)(1-\delta)e+(1-\delta)(\bar{a}-\underline{a})(X_t+x_t)+(\bar{b}-\underline{b})x_t>0,\qquad \bar{a}+\bar{b}<c+d \tag{9.5.2.5}(1−δ)e+(1−δ)(aˉ−a​)(Xt​+xt​)+(bˉ−b​)xt​>0,aˉ+bˉ<c+d(9.5.2.5)

Hence the first best is simple: trade, and conserve in every period, xt=0x_t=0xt​=0. NNN and SSS sign an agreement if and only if it raises their total payoff, and SSS gets a share α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1]α∈[0,1] of the bargaining surplus (as under asymmetric Nash bargaining, or random take-it-or-leave-it offers). Side transfers can thus be used; Section IIE of the paper shows tariffs can replace them. NNN takes no action other than agreeing; SSS's strategy maps histories into xtx_txt​. Propositions 1–3 hold for all subgame perfect equilibria (SPEs); sharper results use Markov perfect equilibria (MPEs) in pure, linear strategies.

The result survives even if liberalization is reversible: once the parties trade, SSS depletes, and after depletion a threat not to trade is not credible.

Contingent Trade Agreements and Renegotiation-Proofness

Once the parties trade, every allocation (τS,τN)(\tau_S,\tau_N)(τS​,τN​) is on the Pareto frontier: any change in τˉ\bar{\tau}τˉ hurts, and is vetoed by, one party. The CTA exploits this multiplicity. Definition 1: a CTA negotiated at TTT specifies tariffs τN(Rt;RT)\tau_N(R_t;R_T)τN​(Rt​;RT​) and τS(Rt;RT)\tau_S(R_t;R_T)τS​(Rt​;RT​) that depend on the current stock RtR_tRt​ (for every Rt∈[0,RT]R_t\in[0,R_T]Rt​∈[0,RT​], including off the equilibrium path) as well as on RTR_TRT​, unless the parties agree on different tariffs. The agreement must give SSS at least its autarky payoff for every RtR_tRt​, and it must be renegotiation proof: the equilibrium payoff pair must be on the Pareto frontier for every feasible RtR_tRt​ at t>Tt>Tt>T. This rules out punishments such as ending SSS's exports after it exploits, since by Proposition 2 trading is always ex post optimal when Rt≤R∗R_t\le R^*Rt​≤R∗. The challenge is that the total gains from trade, e+(aˉ−a‾)Xte+(\bar{a}-\underline{a})X_te+(aˉ−a​)Xt​, rise as XtX_tXt​ rises, so if SSS got a constant fraction of this cake it would have a strong incentive to exploit. The CTA instead lets SSS's share fall with exploitation: SSS's tariff declines in the stock while NNN's rises.

    τˉ(Rt;RT)≥(aˉ+b‾−c)Rt−(aˉ−a‾)R0(9.5.2.15)\bar{\tau}(R_t;R_T)\ge(\bar{a}+\underline{b}-c)R_t-(\bar{a}-\underline{a})R_0 \tag{9.5.2.15}τˉ(Rt​;RT​)≥(aˉ+b​−c)Rt​−(aˉ−a​)R0​(9.5.2.15)

The CTA thus allocates the gains from trade to SSS as long as SSS conserves and to NNN if SSS exploits, and the reallocation is fast enough that conserving dominates. Every allocation remains Pareto efficient ex post, so the scheme is credible: as in Mailath and Samuelson (2006), the punishment rewards the party doing the punishing.

First Best with Export Subsidies

Because conservation is efficient and tariffs serve as side transfers, both parties gain from a CTA that motivates conservation, and they split the surplus according to α\alphaα. Second Best without Subsidies

Export subsidies are generally prohibited by the WTO. Without them, the transfer to SSS is bounded by the gains from trade, which limits how much conservation can be bought.

Comparison with the FTA and Discussion

With a CTA, Propositions 1–5 are overturned: (1) the agreement leads to more conservation than autarky; (2) the agreement is more valuable when RTR_TRT​ is large; (3) SSS conserves to keep the most attractive agreement; (4) in equilibrium SSS conserves when gains from trade are large and RtR_tRt​ is small; (5) τS\tau_SτS​ strictly increases or τN\tau_NτN​ strictly decreases (or both) in RTR_TRT​ and in RtR_tRt​. The CTA yields strictly higher payoffs than the FTA whenever the first best requires conservation but free trade leads to exploitation, aˉ+bˉ−c−d<0<aˉ+bˉ−c\bar{a}+\bar{b}-c-d<0<\bar{a}+\bar{b}-caˉ+bˉ−c−d<0<aˉ+bˉ−c. The online Appendix shows that the equilibrium CTA attains what the parties would obtain if they could commit to a stock-contingent agreement, so it implements the first best with export subsidies and the second best otherwise; it also shows the CTA can be robust to unilateral requests to renege and that exhaustibility is the key assumption. The companion paper Harstad (2024, “Contingent Trade Agreements”) adds nonlinear utilities, noncooperative tariffs as the threat point, and multiple goods and countries, confirms that a CTA is always strictly better than an FTA, and finds in a calibration that a CTA offered by the EU and the US can end or limit deforestation. If the WTO permitted export subsidies for conservation purposes, more forest could be conserved.

This is the resource accounting identity of the model. The state variable is the remaining stock RtR_tRt​ (standing rainforest) at the beginning of period ttt; the control is xt∈[0,Rt]x_t\in[0,R_t]xt​∈[0,Rt​], the amount SSS logs in period ttt; and XtX_tXt​ is the cumulative amount logged before ttt, which is also the area of converted agricultural land and hence SSS's beef output. All three are measured in the same physical units (say hectares), and all are nonnegative.

The first two equalities say that logging moves land one-for-one from the forest account to the agricultural account. The third says that nothing is created or regenerated: the resource is exhaustible, so Xt=R0−RtX_t=R_0-R_tXt​=R0​−Rt​ at every date and one state variable is enough. Iterating the first equality gives

Rt=R0−∑s<txs,Xt=∑s<txs.R_t=R_0-\sum_{s<t}x_s,\qquad X_t=\sum_{s<t}x_s .Rt​=R0​−s<t∑​xs​,Xt​=s<t∑​xs​.

The absence of regrowth rules out any steady state with positive extraction; the only long-run outcomes are conservation of some level R≥0R\ge0R≥0 forever. This is what makes punishments delicate: once the forest is gone the damage is sunk and cannot be undone, which drives the results in equations (6)–(8). The identity Xt=R0−RtX_t=R_0-R_tXt​=R0​−Rt​ is used repeatedly below to rewrite payoffs in terms of RtR_tRt​ alone, for example in equations (7), (9), (14) and (18). The same timing also matters: land logged in period ttt already produces beef in period ttt, which is why flow payoffs in equations (2) and (4) depend on Xt+xtX_t+x_tXt​+xt​.

This is SSS's dynamic programming problem when there is no trade. The flow payoff uSAUTu_S^{AUT}uSAUT​ has three linear pieces. The term (1−δ)(Xt+xt)a‾(1-\delta)(X_t+x_t)\underline{a}(1−δ)(Xt​+xt​)a​ is the value of the beef produced this period on all land converted so far, including land converted this period. The term b‾xt\underline{b}x_tb​xt​ is the one-time domestic value of the timber logged in ttt, and cxtcx_tcxt​ is the one-time cost of logging (possibly including SSS's own discounted environmental loss).

The factor (1−δ)(1-\delta)(1−δ) is a normalization that makes a‾\underline{a}a​ a present-discounted value: a unit of land converted today yields (1−δ)a‾(1-\delta)\underline{a}(1−δ)a​ in every period from now on, worth

∑s=0∞δs(1−δ)a‾=a‾.\sum_{s=0}^{\infty}\delta^{s}(1-\delta)\underline{a}=\underline{a}.s=0∑∞​δs(1−δ)a​=a​.

Hence a‾\underline{a}a​, b‾\underline{b}b​ and ccc are all stock values per unit of land and can be added directly: the net private value of logging one unit in autarky is a‾+b‾−c\underline{a}+\underline{b}-ca​+b​−c. This is the single number that determines the solution in equation (3).

Linearity buys closed forms (bang-bang policies and value functions linear in RtR_tRt​) at the cost of ruling out interior, smoothly varying extraction; the companion paper relaxes it. The value function that solves this Bellman equation, verified in the panel of equation (3), is

VSAUT(Rt)=a‾Xt+max⁡{0, a‾+b‾−c}Rt.V_S^{AUT}(R_t)=\underline{a}X_t+\max\{0,\ \underline{a}+\underline{b}-c\}R_t .VSAUT​(Rt​)=a​Xt​+max{0, a​+b​−c}Rt​.

VSAUT(Rt)=a‾Xt+max⁡{0, a‾+b‾−c}Rt.V_S^{AUT}(R_t)=\underline{a}X_t+\max\{0,\ \underline{a}+\underline{b}-c\}R_t .VSAUT​(Rt​)=a​Xt​+max{0, a​+b​−c}Rt​.

These are the remaining flow payoffs. The first line is SSS's payoff once trade is open: it has the same structure as uSAUTu_S^{AUT}uSAUT​ in equation (2), but beef and timber are now valued at NNN's willingness to pay, aˉ≥a‾\bar{a}\ge\underline{a}aˉ≥a​ and bˉ≥b‾\bar{b}\ge\underline{b}bˉ≥b​. The reason is the pricing assumption: the seller sets the price, so SSS charges NNN's full willingness to pay and captures the whole surplus on its exports. The cost ccc is unchanged.

The second line is NNN's payoff. NNN owns a good that it values at e‾\underline{e}e​ and that SSS values at eˉ\bar{e}eˉ (both present-discounted, hence the factor (1−δ)(1-\delta)(1−δ) per period); in autarky NNN consumes it, under trade NNN sells it at SSS's willingness to pay, gaining e=eˉ−e‾e=\bar{e}-\underline{e}e=eˉ−e​. NNN gets no consumer surplus from SSS's beef or timber because it pays its full valuation. The term −dxt-dx_t−dxt​ is the environmental damage: it is a one-time charge of ddd per unit logged, equivalent to losing a flow (1−δ)d(1-\delta)d(1−δ)d forever. Note that ddd enters NNN's payoff identically with and without trade, so it is only through SSS's behaviour that trade affects NNN's damage.

Two features matter later. First, payoffs are linear and utility is transferable, so only the sum of payoffs determines whether an agreement is signed; this gives the gains from trade in equation (5). Second, with trade the private value to SSS of logging one unit rises from a‾+b‾−c\underline{a}+\underline{b}-ca​+b​−c to

aˉ+bˉ−c ≥ a‾+b‾−c,\bar{a}+\bar{b}-c\ \ge\ \underline{a}+\underline{b}-c ,aˉ+bˉ−c ≥ a​+b​−c,

while the external cost ddd is ignored by SSS in both regimes. This wedge produces equation (6).

The first expression is the per-period gain from trade, obtained by adding the two countries' flow payoffs under an FTA and subtracting the same sum in autarky, holding the extraction xtx_txt​ fixed. From equations (2) and (4),

uSFTA−uSAUT=(1−δ)(Xt+xt)(aˉ−a‾)+(bˉ−b‾)xt,uNFTA−uNAUT=(1−δ)(eˉ−e‾)=(1−δ)e.\begin{aligned} u_S^{FTA}-u_S^{AUT}&=(1-\delta)(X_t+x_t)(\bar{a}-\underline{a})+(\bar{b}-\underline{b})x_t,\\ u_N^{FTA}-u_N^{AUT}&=(1-\delta)(\bar{e}-\underline{e})=(1-\delta)e . \end{aligned}uSFTA​−uSAUT​uNFTA​−uNAUT​​=(1−δ)(Xt​+xt​)(aˉ−a​)+(bˉ−b​)xt​,=(1−δ)(eˉ−e​)=(1−δ)e.​

The cost cxtcx_tcxt​ and the damage dxtdx_tdxt​ cancel because they do not depend on the trade regime. Adding the two lines gives

(1−δ)e+(1−δ)(aˉ−a‾)(Xt+xt)+(bˉ−b‾)xt,(1-\delta)e+(1-\delta)(\bar{a}-\underline{a})(X_t+x_t)+(\bar{b}-\underline{b})x_t ,(1−δ)e+(1−δ)(aˉ−a​)(Xt​+xt​)+(bˉ−b​)xt​,

which is nonnegative because e≥0e\ge0e≥0, aˉ≥a‾\bar{a}\ge\underline{a}aˉ≥a​ and bˉ≥b‾\bar{b}\ge\underline{b}bˉ≥b​, and strictly positive as soon as one of these gaps is strict and the corresponding quantity is positive. So for a given extraction path trade is always efficient.

The second expression is an assumption. To see what it delivers, compute the joint value of logging one more unit when the parties trade: SSS gets the present value of beef aˉ\bar{a}aˉ plus timber bˉ\bar{b}bˉ minus the cost ccc, and NNN suffers ddd, so the joint marginal value is

aˉ+bˉ−c−d<0.\bar{a}+\bar{b}-c-d<0 .aˉ+bˉ−c−d<0.

∂VSCTA(Rt)∂Rt≥b‾−c∀Rt≤RT.\frac{\partial V_S^{CTA}(R_t)}{\partial R_t}\ge\underline{b}-c\qquad\forall R_t\le R_T .∂Rt​∂VSCTA​(Rt​)​≥b​−c∀Rt​≤RT​.

Two ingredients are combined: the slope condition of equation (14) and a participation constraint at the lowest stock. The right side is what SSS gets by logging everything and consuming at home. The construction parallels equation (9), with the CTA replacing the FTA. Under a CTA signed at TTT, SSS conserves, all gains from trade are realized on the existing land, and NNN suffers no further damage, so the total payoff is
